content: The safety and efficacy of using a 3% solution for surgical irrigation in children under 12 years of age have not been established. For individuals aged 12 years and older, the recommended dosage is 15 mL of a 70% solution or 10–20 mL orally every 2 hours until diarrhea occurs. This interaction was observed in a pediatric study (ARROW trial), where children receiving sorbitol-containing lamivudine oral solution had lower plasma lamivudine levels, reduced rates of virologic suppression, and more frequent development of viral resistance compared to those receiving lamivudine tablets. It is advised to avoid or use an alternative drug in such cases. The combination of sodium polystyrene sulfonate and sorbitol has been associated with cases of colonic necrosis, though the exact mechanism is unknown. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative therapy. Both sorbitol and deflazacort can lower serum potassium levels, so caution and close monitoring are necessary when these drugs are used together. Similarly, the combination of dichlorphenamide and sorbitol can increase the toxicity of either drug due to pharmacodynamic synergy, potentially causing metabolic acidosis. Therapy should be modified, and patients should be closely monitored in such cases. Excessive use of sorbitol may lead to side effects such as diarrhea, dehydration, fluid and electrolyte imbalances, hyperglycemia, lactic acidosis, dry mouth, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and nausea. In cases of irrigation, it may cause acute abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or symptoms resembling appendicitis or undiagnosed abdominal pain. Patients with severe cardiopulmonary or renal impairment should use sorbitol with caution, as large volumes may result in fluid overload and electrolyte disturbances. Patients should consult a healthcare professional if they are taking mineral oil, experience a sudden change in bowel habits lasting more than two weeks, or have diabetes, as sorbitol may cause hyperglycemia. If rectal bleeding or no bowel movement occurs after using this product, patients should stop use and seek medical advice, as these could indicate a serious condition. In the event of an overdose, immediate medical attention or contact with a Poison Control Center is necessary. Sorbitol is metabolized primarily in the liver to fructose and has poor absorption when administered orally or rectally. Pregnant women can generally use sorbitol safely, as controlled studies have shown no evidence of fetal risk. Healthcare professionals should exercise caution when prescribing sorbitol to patients unable to metabolize it effectively. Additionally, patients should be informed about potential risks and advised to seek medical guidance if they experience adverse effects.
